author: NorthEast News Desk
body: New Hampshire’s place in video-game history is receiving renewed attention 60 years after engineer Ralph Baer put his idea for interactive television games on paper. Baer wrote a four-page concept on September 1, 1966, while working for Sanders Associates in Nashua.

The document proposed using a television set for play rather than passive viewing. Back in New Hampshire, Baer worked with engineers Bill Harrison and Bill Rusch to turn the concept into experimental systems, culminating in the wood-grain unit that became known as the Brown Box.

Sanders licensed the technology to Magnavox, which released the Odyssey in 1972. The system is widely recognized as the first commercial home video-game console and helped establish a consumer industry that now spans consoles, computers, phones and online platforms.

Baer continued inventing after the Odyssey and became known as the father of home video games. The Smithsonian preserves his early document, prototypes and workshop materials. The anniversary connects an everyday form of entertainment to engineering work carried out in Nashua and Manchester during the 1960s.
dek: A four-page concept written in September 1966 led to the Brown Box prototype and the first commercial home video-game console.
headline: New Hampshire marks 60 years since Ralph Baer’s home-game blueprint
